review:
Techland sold out to Tencent. Let this be a reminder to gamers that no matter how beloved your favorite game studio is, sooner or later they'll have a downfall. 

I've been a fan of Dying Light since the first game released in 2015. So it pains me to see one of my favorite series' fall like that with the introduction of microtransactions and garbage live service elements. 

The story in DL2 is somehow worse than the original. While DL1's story was pretty generic, at least it wasn't crap. DL2's story is more generic and all of its characters are absolutely obnoxious (except for Hakon). I don't know why western devs and movie makers think writing obnoxious characters is good. Don't get me wrong, you can write an entertaining character who's obnoxious, but in DL2 they characters are just obnoxious, not entertaining. 

The combat gameplay in DL2 feels off. When you swing your melee weapons sometimes they don't connect with zombies right in front of you when they should. And the gore seems broken. Even with the Gut Feeling update. The gore might look good but it doesn't feel like its actually tied to the combat. For example, you could drop kick a human enemy and somehow all of their hands and legs would rip off after hitting a wall which makes no sense. Somehow DL1's gore is more realistic. With DL2 being a Chinese game now I think the gore might get downgraded later on. 

I might be a minority on this one but I never really had any complaints about the parkour. I thought it was a definite improvement over the first game and with the Good Night, Good Luck update they improved it even further. I also don't mind the lack of guns in the game. DL was always focused on melee combat and the lack of guns makes the game more challenging whereas in DL1 nighttime became a joke as soon as you got a powerful shotgun where you could also buy ammo for very cheap instead of it being scarce like in Resident Evil. But being OP and shooting volatiles was still fun in its own way NGL. 

Speaking of night, it's laughable how initially Techland completely nerfed the night time experience just to appeal to casuals. Instead of making the night scarier and more complex in DL2 for the millions of fans of DL1 they thought it was a good idea to appeal to people who dropped the game because they were scared of playing a HORROR game. I'm sure the devs had fun wasting their time reworking a core mechanic of the game months after the game was already out when they could've avoided this altogether if they didn't have the bright idea to remove roaming volatiles. But at least they added them back in and made it similar to how it worked in DL1 though it's not perfect yet. It's BS that volatiles NEED to be hit a certain amount of time before they die now. It feels like artificial difficulty. 

To Techland's credit, they did add a community map creation feature which I think more devs should do for their games. Even if DLC2 sucks and Elyseum is never included in the game, fans can now make their own maps and modes and have fun. I hope they keep expanding on this feature. It's also nice that Techland actually listens to feedback and include requested features as soon as they can. They promised at least 5 years of support and before the buyout it really did seem possible. 

I really wanted to love Dying Light 2. And I still do to some extent. But the game fails to live up to the first game even over a year after its release. And after the buyout, I don't think this game will ever do. My hype for DLC2 is almost zero. But that's only because I know almost nothing about the DLC except leaks and rumors as Techland didn't announce anything. I really hope this won't affect the updates Techland makes to change the game for the better but at this point I'm not sure anymore.

I started Dying Light 2 having been a huge fan of Dying Light 1. Let me refresh your memory about Dying Light 1:
Dying Light 1 was a wonderful experience that I put about sixty hours in to, and I enjoyed almost every second of it. 

The dialogue was cheesy, the plot had holes, yes, there are legitimate criticisms you can easily levy at DL1, but I would still overwhelmingly recommend it because, above all else, it was fun. 

The combat felt fantastic, with real weight to your swings. The parkour made you feel agile and, once mastered, gave a real freedom to your movements. There was variety in the environments, with a pleasing amount of verticality. You were free to "grind" to increase your power almost to an unlimited level. And night time felt different - you were genuinely at risk at night, because it brought out much scarier, seriously powerful zombies who would tear you limb from limb if they caught you.

It's worth setting the scene like this, because Dying Light 2 let me down on almost every count.

I didn't expect the story to be any good; there's no pedigree of decent storytelling here. But the devs have shoehorned in an arbitrary choice system so you can "fundamentally change the world". But there isn't actually a branching story tree, they tell the exact same story regardless of your choices, but they have to work the plot around whether you decide to let a few characters live or die - the result of this is that you are left with an impossibly generic story with utterly forgettable characters. 

Sure, the story is terrible, but DL1 wasn't exactly good. It made up for that with fantastic gameplay. So how does that compare here?

In short, not well. DL2 manages to miss the mark in both combat and parkour. The combat feels cartoonish; slapping a zombie or a person with a wrench makes a light bonking sound and often barely staggers the target. It feels a little bit like you're hitting people with foam weapons - until you randomly land a critical hit (which is in no way influenced by an accurate strike, such as to the head, and so doesn't feel rewarding), at which point you will decapitate them, or literally cut them in half with the same weapon that they were completely ignoring a moment ago. 

I think the developers were concerned about how powerful it was possible to get in DL1, and to compensate, levelling now requires picking up a collectable (inhibitors) rather than purely being earned from experience. And they gate the availability of these inhibitors behind map progression, and thus story. Enemies in each subsequent area therefore get harder at the same rate you do, and so this removes any actual sense of progression or power scaling - it takes the same number of hits to kill a zombie at the end of the game as the start. Except it sort of made sense it took three to five hits to kill a zombie with a rusty pipe you've picked up in desperation at the start of the game, and doesn't make much sense that a "legendary" rarity machete that you've modified to both shock and burn takes up to five hits to kill a VISUALLY IDENTICAL zombie. The only difference is that the small number at the top left of their health bar is higher. At least in DL1, as tougher zombies were introduced, they were visually distinct (and you were free to scale as you wished).

The parkour is unfortunately not a redeeming feature here either. In DL2, the movement feels wrong, somehow. You're too floaty, you have no inertia at all. You can jump too high, you can spin 180 degrees at full sprint. It just doesn't feel like any of your movements are particularly deliberate or consequential. 

The streets are just a little too wide; you can't jump across them without having to catch yourself on the edge without using a specific skill, and using that skill drains your stamina, so you can't string freerunning across the city without stopping. 

In DL1, freerunning across the city was a joy; the buildings within a district were usually of subtly different heights, so you're navigating vertically whilst moving across rooftops quickly - this kept the running engaging and fun. In DL2, the buildings are the exact same height. You only have to actually do any parkour to jump across a street when the row of buildings you're on has run out. 

In the second area, buildings are suddenly extremely tall, and this feels immensely promising. But they then immediately introduce the hang glider... This tool (until upgraded) is immensely slow and unresponsive. It leaves you floating slowly in the air as you drift towards your target, but you have absolutely no option of getting around any other way. And once it IS upgraded, you can fly at a reasonable speed more or less indefinitely. So movement has gone from DL1, where you would climb a building, run across rooftops, leaping between them, navigating up and down as you went, with buildings also built on hills and slopes, with destructible roofs and surfaces that make noise and attract risk, to DL2, where you take a lift to the top of the nearest building, then glide directly to your target in an uninteractive way. 

Techland has tried to make DL1 again. They've changed very little about the game and added a few additional features, that, on paper make it more fun.
But all they have succeeded in doing is removing the joy from the experience of playing the game. 

Fans of DL1 will absolutely be able to play through the game. I did, it took me 30 hours of sporadic play. But when I got to the end, I was disappointed, and all I could think was "man, Dying Light 1 was a fun game".

As an old returning player coming back to Dying Light 2 after two years away, I am absolutely furious. I bought the game on Steam again to support the developers and experience the story from the beginning, only to discover that Techland has completely gutted the original opening prologue. The walk through the forest mansion with Spike, the Kyle Crane lore drop, and the intense first-night chase are all gone. These weren't meaningless tutorial scenes they were a huge part of the atmosphere, storytelling, and emotional foundation of the game.

What makes this so frustrating is the reasoning behind it. If the goal was to help new players who just want to jump straight into co-op, YOU ALREADY HAD A “SKIP PROLOGUE” BUTTON! Why permanently remove the content instead of simply letting players choose? Anyone who wanted to skip the opening could already do so, while players who actually wanted to experience the story could enjoy it. There was no reason to take that choice away from everyone.

The original prologue also served an important purpose narratively. It built the tension gradually, established the world, gave context to Aiden's journey, and connected the experience to the history of the franchise. Removing that buildup doesn't just make the game shorter it makes the opening feel hollow and creates gaps that hurt the immersion.

I genuinely appreciate the visual upgrades and physics improvements, but it's incredibly frustrating to see those improvements come alongside the removal of content that gave the game character. After supporting Dying Light since the beginning, coming back two years later expecting to relive that experience and finding out that part of it has simply been erased is deeply disappointing.

You didn't need to remove the prologue. You needed to let players choose whether they wanted to skip it.New players could have skipped it, and longtime fans could have experienced the story the way it was originally designed. That choice should never have been taken away.

Dying Light 2 starts fresh and while it references the first game in its series plenty, it didn't allow itself to be written into a corner by what may have been holding Dying Light 1 back. I obtained the Deluxe edition for £80 and this is what I've found.

[b]Content.[/b]

The voice acting was alright, even good at times. Jonah Scott does a great job, but the story is neither here nor there. It could be a lot worse, but it could be a lot better, too. I don't think anyone is here for a good story, though. The story is just there to pad the world out, make it feel more alive. It serves that purpose just fine. We're here for the parkour, we're here for the zombies, and on this front Techland really delivers. I hope they'll bring back "Be The Zombie" mode. I felt like the mode fell a little flat in Dying Light 1 so if they do I hope they bring something fresh.

[b]Lore.[/b]

In the first one, almost everyone was infected and needed to take antizen to stave off the infection. I believe this was done so that the player could be bitten by a zombie without turning and having people wonder why the player character didn't turn. It's also a good way of avoiding the old cliché of the protagonist being immune. However, on the downside, you never physically saw the protagonist taking antizen, and it also wasn't a mechanic that you needed to manage.
In Dyling Light 2, everyone is infected by a different strain of the virus and this time UV light staves off the infection. So it uses the same concept but in this case you physically have to keep fighting the infection using sunlight or UV light. It's easy enough to manage and actually feels more like a slight inconvenience, but that mindset has got me caught with my pants down a few times where I didn't keep an eye on the timer and had to run for UV-light. You can actually carry around UV-glowsticks that'll work in a pinch, so when I get a bit further into the game and get better equipped this mechanic won't even be an issue.

[b]Technical.[/b]

I've experienced quite a few bugs, and several game breaking bugs. A few zombie corpses started T-posing on me, a few times I didn't hear audio, I've had enemies wander around inside cutscenes, once it even skipped an objective for a mission for me. I've had missions that I was unable to progress in because of a soft lock which resolved itself after I abandoned it and tried a different mission instead. I was forced to close my game once when I was instructed to scout Jack & Joe's camp using binoculars only it wouldn't unequip the binoculars no matter what I did. Force-closing the game in this instance caused me to lose a lot of progress.

When it comes to video game developers you should not trust promises but rather look at their track record to determine their integrity. With the bugs I've found I would normally suggest you do not buy it, at least until those bugs are fixed. However, with Techland I feel reassured that these bugs will be fixed in due time. This is because Dying Light 1 got support for years through multiple DLCs and a plethora of updates and bug-fixes. It's up to you if you want to trust that the bugs will be addressed and buy it while it's essentially a late stage early-access, but I'm pretty confident in my purchase.

I have 16 hours at the time of writing this, so it's up to you to decide whether or not that's long enough to have gotten a feel for the game and write an accurate review, but I'll be playing it much longer and I'll update this review accordingly.

Update #2:

I am now on my second playthrough to experience a different ending, and unfortunately I have to say that the bug I experienced in my first playthrough where a bunch of my progress was wiped happened again. This time I was not forced to force-close the game but actually closed the game properly. Right around the quest 'Unruly Brother' I found the same issues I did on my first playthrough, where I would be unable to progress in the main story quest unless I first did another side quest to force the game to check and update the journal again to recognise that the main quest requirements for progression had been satisfied.

When I closed the game by going through the main menu it instead just closed the game and I lost a bunch of progression yet again. I had hoped that in my first playthrough these issues were just a fluke and perhaps even unique to my experience. But it seems that this bug happens consistently. Let me reiterate this so that you may keep this in mind when making your purchase; This game's state is essentially a late-stage early access. This game is not complete.

As a final note I have to mention the free DLC packs. Why is it given to us in 3 parts when this DLC in its entirety isn't more than just a single outfit? Why are the stats on these items no longer relevant after 2 hours? Why not just release it as a cosmetic skin instead? Thank you but this is worthless. I get that Techland probably had these outfits ready around the time they released the game and are now drip-feeding the content to maintain the playerbase's intrigue and the release's momentum, but this is time they could've spent fixing the countless gamebreaking bugs. Buyer beware.

Initially I was on the fence about this game. I loved dying light 1 a lot. I thought the mix of horror + parkour+ melee combat was refreshing and the gameplay was very well done. When I first got dying light 2 I felt a little down as the game launched in a "half-baked" state. The melee system felt like it took a step backwards and the performance/bugs were intrusive to the gameplay. Then I remembered that the same thing happened with dying light 1, and Techland fixed that with some patches + time. The EXACT same thing has happened with dying light 2. Now with reloaded edition and all the updates it has, the game is very, very good. I won't comment on story because some people like it some people don't. Its very preference based. Gameplay-wise however, almost everything is better than dying light 1. The only gripe I have is the blueprint system feels a little weird. I preferred the system in dying light 1. Levelling up blueprints feels a little worse/not as good as finding a high level blueprint in the wild. 

Here's a quick breakdown of the different gameplay aspects:

Parkour: PHENOMENAL. so much creativity and player expression in how you move around. Playing in CO-OP was awesome because you get to see how your friend(s) take different routes to get to the same destination.

Melee: VERY GOOD. Feels kinda wonky if the enemies out level you a lot but once I got used to the swing animation and the moment physics it was great. Weighty weapons felt weighty, speedy weapons felt speedy. Hit registration felt good even in CO-OP 

Night-time: VERY GOOD. Chases can be annoying when trying to do nighttime objectives but the actual atmosphere and tension of night time is very well executed.

Map-Design:  VERY GOOD/PHENOMENAL I won't spoil the story but all areas of game felt well designed and always fun to traverse Having your actions impact the world was also very cool to see. 

Story: PRETTY DECENT. Might be kinda cliche but the morally grey world presented was pretty cool imo. Had to really, think about who I help. The results of your choices may or may not be significant but at least you get to see the consequences. Game also is good in length. It can be speedrunned but for a first play through I think that defeats the purpose of an RPG. 

UI/Inventory: GOOD. UI was good. Nothing major/crazy but it works. Can be hard to see other players in COOP but I have bad eyes.  Having weapon dmg scale was nice if you find a weapon you like. It could be bad if the weapon you like doesn't scale (I had a police baton I liked but it was stuck at lvl 6).

TL:DR   Dying Light 2 Reloaded Edition is 100% WORTH THE PRICE OF ADMISSION. The game works, works well, and is a blast to play.  HIGHLY RECOMMEND

Sorry, this is kinda harsh.

- Weaker atmosphere and soundtrack. Aside from the combat this is the biggest sentiment I see mirrored online.
- Weapons can still be upgraded but no longer crafted
- The hang glider feels kinda clunky and slow despite being one of the very few additions I can name, and its usage is enforced in many late game areas
- No x-ray damage in combat
- No PvP, which the first game had in the form of the "Be the Zombie" mode
- Enemies are generally less frightening to fight, with the nighttime being more of an inconvenience than the omnipresent terror that gave the series its literal tagline, given that volatiles don't come out unless you've been alerting the new and annoying-as-all-hell screaming enemies too much. Even the virals that would chase you at all hours of the day don't seem to be an issue unless you alert the screamers at night. These screamers are also almost entirely at street level, meaning that if you stick to the rooftops, which you usually do, then "night" basically doesn't exist-- effectively removing one of the most challenging, frightening, and iconic parts of the first game. In fact, the game has lots of missions and areas that encourage or require you to explore ground-level buildings at night, implying they're aware of this issue. Not only that, you have an upgradable immunity timer that outright KILLS YOU if you spend too long in the dark now. It literally feels like they're trying to cheat to get to the same experience.
- No real guns this time around
- Enemies have levels and health bars for some reason. This is toggle-able and obviously a callback to Dead Island but it feels really out of place
- [EDIT: apparently they added a new gore system recently, so much of this is probably outdated, but that was added like a year after the fact so I am not going back to try it out] Blood and gore effects are far less visceral both in sound and presentation. Combat in general just isn't as punchy. I went out of my way to engage in combat in DL1 just to see the enemies' bodies getting damaged and to experience the cool ambient screaming and slow motion effects that would highlight intense kills, but now I just avoid it because the exciting bits are just absent. I would try to explain all the tiny details but just look up comparisons on YouTube-- there's a bunch.
- No vehicles, unlike in the original's DLC
- Choices "impact the world" as much as any other cookie cutter open world game, despite this being a major selling point during the original advertising run. Yes there are faction choices and some light upgrade decisions that impact the open world's structures, but this really isn't new or that impactful
- Very few new additions that really set the game apart, including an underwhelming skill tree that doesn't feel like it added anything the first game didn't have
- On that note, another one of the only things pushed as an improvement is the parkour, which feels very odd since the parkour was one of the strongest aspects of the first game. As such, the handful of new parkour moves and the improved responsiveness feel like only a marginal improvement since I don't recall anyone really complaining before outside of certain climbing sections. I would've liked to see them focus on the weaker elements like the poor story, forgettable side quests, and the removed systems instead of polishing something that could've realistically been left mostly as-is.
- Somewhat buggy in my experience
- Me and my friend were going to play this game together originally, but unlike the first game, co-op progress is not saved between players
- A story that seemed to show some promise initially that fell to the same lows (or lower) as the original by the end, with weak and underutilized characters being at the forefront. 
- The same two-map structure as the first game, added verticality in the second half of the game and all. Except this time it's skyscrapers instead of multi-story buildings meaning it's less about parkour and more about figuring out how to get around with the hang glider and the ziplines, which is far more tedious and involves much less combat
- A new main character that is so embarrassingly similar to the original I mistakenly thought they had the same voice actor.

I literally had to take a step back and wonder if the first game was even as good as I remembered. That's how disappointing this game felt. Every change feels pointless, either because it removes something that made the first game so good or adds something that doesn't make up for it.

I can understand why people like the game, given that it isn't really *objectively* bad, but it is a 100%, unarguable downgrade from the first game. Aside from having less fun in general, it was very hard to tell what was wrong with the game while I was playing, but I began to realize what I liked so much about the original as I watched video comparisons. 

Ironically, this game is what I imagined the first game would be like upon first purchasing it-- the underwhelming, forgettable drop in the open world/zombie ocean it miraculously wasn't.

I think that is the underlying issue. People totally slept on Dying Light 1 *because* it looked relatively generic and uninteresting. It had a special charm that made it so enjoyable from its desolate sepia streets filled with particle and sound ambiance, droning synth soundtrack, black-spattered UI, horrifying volatile night encounters, realistic and shambling zombies, and the undeniably punchy and *squelchy* combat that was filled with many fun effects. Even the buggy in The Following DLC was a contentious issue because people thought it'd take away from the fun parkour, but it added a whole new system to play with and use to kill whole hordes of enemies-- whereas the hang glider in this game really does feel like it slows down the movement and combat. At no point during this game (aside from possibly the slightly stronger story buildup) did I feel this game was iterating on the original. I would be very hard pressed to list what has been added over the original game, but I found myself waiting for it to be *as* good as the original with its systems and presentations. And then the game ended. 

Dying Light 1 was *unexpectedly* good. Especially with its weak story, it teetered on being underwhelming, but it beat the odds. Trying that luck again was simply too ballsy and that lightning didn't strike twice.

I read Endie's positive review of the game and I really like the first line:

        "I think TechLand actually shot themselves in the foot with Dying Light 2 by making 
     Dying Light first."

because that's exactly my opinion of this game and why I can't recommend it. If a sequel isn't even going to be *as* good as the original, nor try anything significantly different, then what's the point? Why remove mechanics and core aspects of the presentation? Why make a heart-pounding zombie survival game easier and less frightening? Why do any of this while keeping the game's scope virtually unchanged? It ends up feeling like a weaker attempt at remaking the same game. If you haven't played a Dying Light game, play the first. If you have, then I can't think of a reason to play this.

In a bizarre decision techland decided to "reduce" the prologue by over 2 hours, and "sanitized" a few initial cutscenes, in an effort to quickly allow the players to dive into the game. I had not played this game before the update, and when I played through the prologue myself, I could feel something seriously off about it. Tutorials are weird, there are pauses in some scenes as if the player is expected to make a choice but are presented with none, and of course, one huge story character has been entirely removed.

The reduction is asinine, to the point of being fraud. If you buy the game today looking at trailers and youtube walkthroughs etc, you'll bet getting a drastically different experience for the first two to three hours. Here's a full list of things removed.

Several minutes of early content has been removed, including:
[list]
 [*]Meeting Spike
 [*]Harran references and easter eggs
 [*]Conversations about the end of the world
 [*]Early parkour tutorials
 [*]The Banshee encounter
 [*]Aiden's nightmare dream sequence
 [/list]
Overall prologue length has been reduced by roughly an hour and now takes around 45 to 50 minutes.
The opening cutscene with Aiden collecting the radio now plays automatically without player input. New zombies have been added to the early area and some mission objectives have changed. After reaching the church, players must kill zombies and gather Honey and Chamomile to unlock the Medicine blueprint.

But there are even more bizarre changes:
[list]
 [*]Spike no longer teaches medicine crafting. Aiden figures it out himself.
 [*]Some previously accessible areas are now blocked off with barricades.
 [*]The first parkour skill unlocks after entering the tunnel.
 [*]The first combat skill unlocks after the player's first kill.
 [*]The Vault Kick tutorial has been removed. Players can ignore the skill entirely and continue the story.
 [*]Fighting practice against Renegades is now optional instead of mandatory.
 [*]The Bazaar hanging scene has been censored, showing only a black screen instead of the full sequence.
 [*]Hakon and Biomarker Section
 [*]The crystal container near Hakon has been removed.
 [*]Opening the GRE crate now happens during daytime.
 [*]The GRE crate no longer contains loot.
 [*]Aiden no longer suffers a seizure after opening the crate.
 [*]Entire Chase Sequence Removed
[/list]

The following events have been completely cut:
[list]
 [*]The night chase back to the Bazaar.
 [*]Being denied entry because Aiden lacks a biomarker.
 [*]The famous Volatile scream cutscene.
 [*]The rooftop fight sequence.
[/list]
 Instead, Hakon immediately tells Aiden to meet him at the GRE Hospital to obtain a biomarker.

Dialogue Changes
[list]
[*]Several conversations with Hakon have been shortened.
[*]The dialogue choices regarding what Aiden will do after finding Mia have been removed.
[*]The game now automatically chooses the line about settling down somewhere.
[*]Additional dialogue about Aiden's future plans has been cut.
[/list]

Hakon still gives Aiden binoculars, but the tutorial that previously required marking the Windmill and the Bazaar has been removed.

It's a good game, but its not great. DL1 was 100% better than this game, and its pretty disappointing. The parkour is better in DL2, and is very fun, but in basically every other department (story, combat, atmosphere, etc), DL1 is just so much better. DL2's combat is fun, don't get me wrong, but it just feels so... empty. In DL1, I used to run around (even at max level in power and legend) and kill zombies for an hour, because it was fun to just mindlessly kill zombies. The combat felt weighty and (semi) realistic, it wasn't perfect, but it was perfect for a game like DL1. In DL2, I actively avoid all forms of combat. It just doesn't feel as good as DL1. Human combat is better, but it still feels kinda weird. 

On top of that, the zombies themselves in DL2 don't feel good at all to fight against. They just walk towards you, take you hits without retaliating, they don't feel even close to as reactive as DL1's zombies. In DL1, the zombies stumbled towards you, as you hit them, your weapon rebounded off of them, as if they're an actual person (in DL2, you slash/strike straight through them, as if you just slightly grazed them, DL1 feels better because it actually feels as if you're slashing/hitting a person/zombie with a weapon, it doesn't phase through them), and if you got too many hits in or got too close, they would grab you or push you away. The zombies actively felt like they wanted to kill you, they were much more reactive (ragdolls were also one the main reasons that the enemies felt so realistic/dynamic in DL1). The gore also felt better, mostly due to DL2 having health bars and levelling systems for combat, which makes it feel like you're not fighting a zombie to kill them, rather that you're trying to deplete their health bar (dismemberment/decapitations only really happen on the last hit an enemy can take or if you get a crit, with a health bar always being above a zombie, it constantly reminds you that you have x amount of hits until you can kill the enemy/zombie, making it seem much less dynamic). 

Also, DL1 had much, much better atmosphere. Harran was great, the slums had a murky and gritty atmosphere, it felt depressing, but great. Old Town felt more refined, and had better rooftop parkour, but still kept the atmosphere that the slums had. Villedor and the Central Loop in DL2 is great, but its missing the atmosphere that the Slums and Old Town had. You could hear the screams of virals in the distance as you run from rooftop to rooftop, as you narrowly avoid zombies below you. The atmosphere in DL1's maps was very palpable, but DL2 doesn't really have that. The maps feel static, and they don't feel alive whatsoever, it just feels like a playground for parkour (which they did very well in that regard, the Central Loop is extremely fun to parkour in). Also, DL1's nights were significantly scarier, the first in DL1, nights were genuinely terrifying. In DL2, you can casually stroll around at night (even at street level), and its not even tense; you can escape chases so easily its not even funny. The only way you can get a high level chase is if you go out of your way to purposefully start it. 


The zombies took a backseat in DL2. It feels less like a zombie game, and more like a post-apocalyptic game with zombies added in there for some background noise. The people in DL2's world don't feel oppressed by zombies, nor concerned by them. In DL1, you could feel how zombies had a real impact on the world and how they were an actual threat to humans; random events of people being attacked by zombies, people in the story and in safe-zones actually talking about zombies and how they pose a real threat to them (like Brecken's night mission that went wrong, you had to set up traps for the night mission to avoid the dangerous zombies/volatiles at night, the game gave you a first hand example of how zombies are dangerous in this world, especially at night, something DL2 doesn't do), and stuff like that. DL2 doesn't really have any of that. 

The story is honestly just not good. The characters, at least to me, were more irritating than anything (especially Lawan). It felt nonsensical at times, and it felt like a slog to progress through. DL1's story, while not great in any way, I still think its better. It felt more serious and realistic (ish), I was genuinely intrigued in the story and I cared for the characters (I didn't care a lot or even moderately, but I certainly cared a lot more for DL1's characters than the characters in DL2). 

Despite the pretty negative things I've said about DL2, I still think its an okay game. I personally (and a lot of other people) think its a step down from DL1 in most departments, but the parkour and world is something to be experienced.

Unfortunately, I can not recommend Dying Light 2 on objective merits alone.

First off:

The Story:

The story is terrible, full of plot holes, and without any actual shred of choice present. Remember the whole "your choices have consequences" marketing bs? Well, in DL2 none of your choices matter all that much, and the ones that do are given to you at the halfway point(vnc tower, and at the X13 mission). Everything else, no matter what you do always stay relatively the same except for a few lines of dialogue  to indicate *something* changed. What changed? No idea, but at least it sounds cool.

This is the same problem that dying light had, but I didn't care as much because the gameplay was top notch. However, I was expecting a stronger emphasis on story, but what we got was a disjointed mess with to many boring characters, and not enough time to form strong relationships with the main characters.

Onto, the side quests! The side quests in Dying Light more than made up for the games mediocre story, as it felt like the sidequests were designed to utilize the gameplay, and especially the parkour system in dl1. However, in DL2 -90% of the sidequests are 'go here fetch that quests', and unlike DL1 there are no interesting npcs to make the quests memorable. The rest are the stupid parkour challenges.. which are not fun. Oh, and one last thing- certain side quests you are locked out by completing the main story which really ***** sucks.

Lastly, the gameplay:

The one perk I will give this game is that the freerunning is vastly improved, and the environment looks beautiful-if a bit to comical in places. However, parkour can be very floaty, and I've lost count of the number of times I've glitched through textures and geometry- subsequently dying as a result. As you can imagine, this gets annoying real fast.

Combat in DL2 is very hit or miss. Combat with humans can be very fluid at times or very clunky as well. There seems to be hit box issues, where enemies can hit you despite you being out of the range of their swings. Every enemy has some sort of power attack, that can interrupt your block-which also does extreme amount of damage.  Hits caused by the player, sometimes are not detected properly, but this has been less of an issue of late.

Now zombie combat is okay, but is does lack the dismemberment that DL1 had. It is still very gory, and enjoyable. Biters now grab you more often which is incredibly annoying- especially if you are in a confined space. The weapon upgrade system is equal parts terrible, and useful but this would be a very long review if I covered all my gripes in detail. The one thing I will say is that having no repair system sucks. 

Night time in DL2 is a lot less scary, and that is not a bad thing. In DL1  there was no point in going out at night as there was no need to and the volatile spam made it less than fun. In DL2 , night can be very dangerous, but I have a reason to actually go out-whereas I did not in Dying Light 1.*

Lastly, health bars suck, and the gear leveling system is meh. Weapon stats are also tied to gear pieces. Thus making the game feel like a ubisoft game. 

There is so much more I would love to go over, but this will suffice for now. 

In summation:

Dying Light 2 is the kind of game that asks a simple question:
“What if parkour was perfect, zombies were everywhere, and your character had the immune system of a wet napkin?”

And honestly? It mostly nails it.

First, the movement. This game makes running across rooftops feel so good that you’ll actively avoid the ground like it owes you money. Vaulting, climbing, sliding—everything flows so smoothly that you’ll forget there’s a fast travel system because why would you ever use it? I came to kill zombies and ended up auditioning for a post-apocalyptic parkour Olympics.

Then there are the zombies, who are doing their absolute best despite clearly being dead. During the day, they’re slow, ugly, and perfect for stress relief. At night, however, they turn into Olympic sprinters with anger issues. The game politely warns you that nighttime is dangerous, and if you ignore it, it teaches you a valuable lesson called instant regret.

The combat is satisfyingly brutal. Smacking a zombie with a metal pipe feels weighty, especially when that pipe breaks mid-fight and forces you to rethink your life choices. Weapon durability is back, because nothing says “survival horror” like watching your favorite machete disintegrate after three enemies and a mild breeze.

The story exists—and that’s not an insult. It gives you choices that feel important, even if sometimes the consequences are “this area is now purple instead of blue.” Still, the world reacts to you enough that you feel responsible for your actions, which is impressive considering you spend most of your time kicking infected off rooftops for fun.

Visually, the game looks great. The city of Villedor is grimy, colorful, and somehow cozy for a place overrun by monsters. The soundtrack knows exactly when to hype you up and when to quietly remind you that you are very alone and mildly doomed.

Dying Light 2 is a fantastic open-world zombie game with top-tier parkour, satisfying combat, and just enough horror to keep your heart rate legally questionable. It’s not perfect, but when a game makes you smile while being chased across rooftops by screaming mutants, it’s doing something very right.

Would definitely risk nighttime again (but complain about it loudly). Score: 8.5/10

Disappointment.

While I commend Techland's effort in trying to elevate Dying Light to not-just-another-open-world-zombie-slasher level, they simply bit off more than they can chew. It's really obvious there's a lot of cut content that were too ambitious to implement properly, some new changes and new mechanics just don't seem to fit in, and while core gameplay remains strong as ever, this game lacks a specific magic from the first installment.

+ Parkour might feel floaty at first, but I really love how it has coyote time everywhere. Crossing any gap is easier than ever, chaining non-context parkour moves is silky smooth and satisfying, and vertical movement now just has as many options as horizontal. This is easily the most improved mechanic from the first game, the abundance of choices in how you traverse Villedor makes this game a different kind of beast compared to any other title in the genre.

+ Combat now incorporate movement much more, with an emphasis on a jump kick move that you unlock early. Wall running or hanging on a horizontal bar allows you to insta-kick or punch which is pretty dope.

- However, in terms of practical improvements, combat doesn't seem to innovate as much as parkour. Fighting against human is a series of red light green light where you wait for enemy to make a move, dodge or parry based on their attack, counter attack, then repeat. The base kick is too slow and doesn't feel good to pull off, so you should rely on dropkick which is powerful, creates goofy result, and simply more satisfying than anything else. But here's the problem, dropkicking is too powerful, to the point that there's no reason for you to not cheese through any human fight with it. Dropkick them out of any 20 story building, dropkick them into a spike wall, dropkick them into idk a wall, sometimes it's an instakill, sometimes it's 3 hits kill and they can't do jack shit against you. It's fun, but unbalanced and has a weird spot in an inadequate combat system.

- Combat against zombie is just, urgh, not fun, really. I don't know exactly what's wrong with it, but enemies just feel much more spongy than ever, even more than in Dead Island. There's a lack of oomph in physics, moves like aerial takedown is now tied to F button instead of just attacking while you're on air, and zombies don't seem to react properly to your attack. It's not bad, but it sometimes feels like a downgrade from DL1.

- There's a severe lack of tension at night. One of the biggest selling points of DL1 was the Volatile threat that had you hauling ass to safe houses if you don't want to lose your stuff, and those chases, while I can understand why some people couldn't stand it, were my most favorite moments in any open world game ever. Here in DL2, the dynamic has changed. At day, most zombies sleep in houses, stores, any place with interior, the streets only contain some roaming biters at best. At night, more of them come out, special zombies appear, which leave the interiors easy to explore and loot. While I liked this change at first, it's just inevitable that night gameplay won't be as satisfying as in the first game due to very simplistic stealth mechanics, and because this dynamic is driven purely by reward, the game passively pushes you into the more boring parts of the game: the empty streets at day, or the empty shops at night.

- This game is too maximalist for my taste. Of course, subtle environmental interaction wasn't the first game's strong suit either, but this game is really designed by icons and HUD elements. I don't need it to be Metro Exodus, but it's not really playable with some icons turned off. Stores used to be able to identify by looking at them, now it's not really possible to tell which one has interiors, so the game marks them on the map for you. The game is overstuffed with information and navigating them is a chore. Since the streets, rooftops, alleys and even interiors blend into each other after a while, it's not easy to reach a specific location without an objective marker. You can miss out on lootable items without using survivor sense, you can miss out on random events (because frankly the audio in this game is not the best) without the blue marker on the screen. It's not possible to play it with minimal HUD aside from enemy's HP bar turned off, because it's not designed for it, which turns exploration into a pretty railroaded breadcrumb chase that's saved by outstanding parkour.

- The entire narrative, plotlines, character writing and C&C are a sham. My emotion after finishing the game is a big fat "who cares" shrug. You don't spend enough time with NPCs who treat you like their best friends, there are too many characters taking turn appearing and aren't used well in the overarching plot, everyone talk and act in the same manner, the whole thing is completely devoid of any stake or emotion and there's nothing that stand out. It's not as weirdly charming as Days Gone, not as stylistically niche and loud as Borderlands, not as focused with a singular theme as the Metro series, not as rich and inventive in its worldbuilding like Death Stranding, not as tightly written filled with sharp ideas like Wasteland 3. Its modern dark age setting has nothing new to present and tackle on, nothing new to say, nothing interesting to hear, nothing personal to touch you in your heart, nothing fierce enough as a statement. For a game that tells you to stay human, its spirit is as anemic and pale as a walking zombie.

It is a competent product that managed to take on cool new ideas despite dealing with gigantic development issues, and for that it is already better than anything from Ubisoft these days. But as someone who adores the first game, this feels like a misstep, a water-down experienced created by blueprints and archetypes.

I loved Dying Light 1, but I like Dying Light 2. Not saying that's an inherently bad thing, the game is incredibly good fun. The parkour combat has been kicked up a notch and the zombies feel a little more dangerous. The rogue people are savages that have better AI and are definitely more fun to fight. The maps are bigger and have more packed in. All this stuff is great, but something about Dying Light 2 feels hollow. Like there's a piece missing that should be there the first game had. 

Then I realized it: The story. The world. It's hollow.

The story didn't feel the same as in Dying Light 1. Sure Dying Light 1's story wasn't all the special, but it was serviceable and really kept you gripped as you fought Rais (or industry standard Vaas clone). The characters were far more consistent and weren't jumping into the story one after the other. They had time to develop a little so you could build some kind of connection. Working for the GRE was the biggest factor in what made DL1 interesting, as you learned of the corruption they were embezzled in.  
Haraan was a fictional city, but you could tell it was based off of the slums of countries like Brazil. As you ran around you could see how the denizens of the Slums did all they could to fend off the infected, but to no avail. Their shanty apartments did little to shelter them. All except the tower, the last safe haven. There was a real "holy shit" moment when you entered Old Town and you knew for a fact this is where all the well off people tried to hide, leaving those in the slums to die. Blocking off tunnels and plugging up hiking routes to contain them. Taking the first rescue rides out. 

Dying Light 2 seems to be missing all of this. How many characters just kept popping up in the story that lose all relevancy later on? Oh hi Sophie, ok bye Sophie. Hi Barney, ok by Barney. Hi Aitor, ok bye Atior. It just kept happening, almost nobody stayed in the story except Hakon, Lawan, Jack, Waltz and Frank. Sophie was there to serve as a tool to move Aiden into the Central Loop. Her whole character is "my mommy died, she was a strong leader i must be like her". Like ok Shonen Protag #12,924.  Almost as if she was meant to be written out. 

The world in Dying Light 2 feels expansive. It feels big, it's packed with stuff to do. At the same time, it doesn't really "show" you what to do. Old Villedor feels so copy pasted that it doesn't have prominent land marks that say "hey, here's the fun!". DL1 did that plenty, notably that bridge that served as climbing challenge. A few larger buildings would have definitely been beneficial.  Central Loop turns it up with the parkour, but it relies heavily on the grappling hook and the paraglider to quickly get around, otherwise running around is a little more dangerous and sluggish. I wish Techland had made unlocking the Central Loop feel like more of a reward, creating areas that can't be glided to and rely strongly on parkour skills. SO SO SO much potential for roof to roof sky scraper parkour and they traded it for flying roof to roof. Enclosed alley ways that give the player a reason to climb and jump through or maybe more sky scrapers that can be scaled from the inside would've been great additions. 

Yeah and optimization is pretty terrible, could've used another delay to iron that mess out.

Over all, buy Dying Light 2 if you want. It's in its own league. You can't really find a game like this that's so fleshed out. There's plenty of fun to be had and I certainly did. I'm not punching in too much more time until they fix the frame rate issues. If you run a high end card you're set.

While not an absolute recommendation, I think this game is worth a buy depending on what you liked from Dying Light 1. Dying Light 2 takes most of Dying Light's basic mechanics and improves on them, while at the same time kinda forgetting a lot other content that was added on over time. I'll start with the negatives, don't expect driving vehicles like in The Following (for now. At the time of this review we only have the base game with no clear indication of what expansion content in planned.). Also don't expect the a lot of gunplay as guns are not a thing anymore with just a small exception of makeshift boomsticks that quickly are used up. The story definitely feels like it was a product of hastily stitched together elements and rewritten multiple times with some easily predictable turns. Progression has gotten way more grindy too, from collecting trophies of infected to upgrade blueprints to getting materials for said blueprints, and hunting down inhibitor injectors to enhance your health and stamina, all on top of DL1's previous leveling and skill tree system makes it a lot to manage and improve to optimize yourself. 

Negatives aside, DL2's parkour skills combined with its revised mechanics have made traversing the world a blast. The grappling hook no longer feel's like it came from Arkham Knight, but lets you swing like Spiderman along the taller cityscapes. Wall running, gliding and sliding through areas make traveling from point to point pretty awesome teamed with music tracks that play along as you keep on the go. Combat is slightly more complex now, where human enemies can see you spamming stuff and learn to defend against it pushing you to do varied stuff to win against a small group of human opponents. Infected are more dangerous as night now, I know some think that DL1's nightfall was more scary and I can agree with that, but volatiles felt still harder to kill in this game than the previous one. Tools you craft are more useful now compared to DL1 thanks to the upgrade system to improve the effects of everything from weapon mods to throwables like UV lights, medicine, and molotovs. As much as the story feels flat, there are decisions you can take that will change the ending or have reaching consequences which is something I hope they further develop in any future content. With cooperative play available, you can bring in up to 3 others to trick off buildings and gang up on enemies.

Overall, I recommend this game for its improved parkour and combat, but note that the campaign doesn't hold up to its previous game. Side quests were good though, and still is fun to jump back into from time to time.

I played Dying Light 1 on release and it immediately became one of my all time favorite games. Not because of the story or the characters but because of the gameplay. The parkour was fluid, the combat was fun and felt rewarding. It all worked because the input detection was functional and straightforward.

It isn't like that in Dying Light 2; whereas you had one button for a kick in DL1 and had press two for a dropkick, you have to make make 2 or 3 inputs respectively for the same actions in DL2. No one asked for it. You can't remap it. It just sits there and clutters up your gameplay. One could argue that it's not that bad and you can work around it and I would agree, but that is just one thing. There are many more dumb input decisions or dumb decisions in general. 

Like grab attacks. Oh how I hate grab attacks in this game. In DL1 zombies would grab you. OCCASIONALLY. The grabs were always clearly telegraphed and it was always by a zombie that was clearly in your FOV, so if you got grabbed it was always you own fault and later in game you could escape the grab with a one button input anyway so it wasn't too annoying. It was easy enough to evade.
In DL2 you get grabbed CONSTANTLY. So much so that I believe the game is getting off on you being grabbed. You are running full speed past a zombie? You get grabbed. You just whacked zombie upside it's head? You get grabbed. You are on top of a car, you are trying to jump and grab onto a ledge, there is a zombie next to the car that can maybe reach your kneecaps? Guess who or what gets grabbed? That's right. Not the ledge. And guess who is lining up another grab while you are busy with the stupid QTE to get out of the first one? You don't have to answer that.
A zombie even managed to grab me through a closed gate. It just noclipped through it in order to grab me. 

Climbing inputs don't work right. In DL1 you could basically keep RB1 pressed and Crane would climb up a wall almost entirely by himself. I don't know what's wrong with Aiden but he never seems to know which ledge to grab onto to climb up. Pressing the crouch button also doesn't let you drop down reliably, so you often end up in situations where you are halfway up a telephone booth and Aiden.exe just stops working while a zombie is whacking away at you, foaming at the mouth to grab you, as soon as you manage to let go.

I was determined to see this game through to the end but I just can't because of the saving system. It reset my progress  by 20-30 minutes severeal times between sessions and during the last mission I played, a group of enemies, that I had to defeat in order to progress, froze up and became unkillable. After killing myself several times and respawning the problem persisted. I opted to return to the main menu and continue the game from there only to find that over an hour of progress had been deleted. I closed the game and I doubt I will ever play it again.

If you want to play a fun zombie-dropkicking game I would suggest you play the first Dying Light. Skip this one.

- Only some choices feel like they matter, and even then it's a bit "meh".

Bad:

- Character progression, loot and stats are a bit weak. You CAN pick and choose skills while leveling, but all characters are the same when maxed. Gear stats do make some difference, but level scaling still makes the zombies feel stronger as you grow, instead of you feeling stronger as you grow.
- Parkour is janky: Sometimes you grab onto thing you never intended to.
- Parkour is janky: Sometimes you can't grab onto something because it only looks like it's grabbable or the hitbox where you CAN grab onto it was somewhere else. Example: You can grab ropes, except the ropes that are intended as a lift service. These ropes look just like any other rope, but you cannot grab onto them except for the entrypoints at the top and bottom. You will fall to your death.
- Parkour is janky: Sometimes you get flung backwards, around and forwards again, going everywhere because the automatic grabbing and move-mechanisms can't translate your inputs to what is in the world
- Animations are super jittery on high refresh monitors, almost as if they are stuck in 60 fps and the 165Hz makes them freak out. Zombies sometimes start vibrating violently during animations. There are lots of weird offsets occuring, like your hands clearly not being where the animator intended etc.
- Performance issues in some cases. Certain areas seem to stay well below 60 fps steady, even if I can run most of the game above 100 fps steady.
- "Choices matter". Sure. Make one choice to have 1 cutscene play, and the other choice to have another cutscene play. Well, some choices do matter, but to me it seems mostly about the color of the flag in the bases. You also don't always have any reason to pick one choice over the other, outside of "Eh, this person feels more trustworthy based on the shape of their face".
- For a game that revolves around climbing on rooftops, there are a lot of rooftops that are unclimbable. Huge collision boxes simply block you from going on some roofs. The parkour mechanisms freak out and you will fall to your death.
- Every weak zombie has the strongest move in the game: "Grab onto you and force you to sit through a 4 second unskippable animation"
- Some athletic zombies can pounce you to the ground. They also do this around corners (even 180 degrees), through some walls and through the blade of your swinging weapon.
- No guns (disregarding one weak and barely useful exception)
- Can't repair weapons. Unless, of course, you LIKE using a weak weapon until it needs to be repaired to become stronger. Just slap the upgrades on first chance you get and enjoy the strong weapon instead.
- Molotovs are barely putting a dent in zombies health, only useful against super weak zombies and to stun renegades so you can heal
- Weak story. I find myself skipping a lot of it, leading to missing a few interesting parts by accident. A lot seems to be short and low effort attempts at pulling at the players heartstrings.
- You can actually climb a lot of the tallest building quite early in the game, abusing the jankyness of the parkour to your advantage. Don't though, it's reserved for a crucial main story quest.
- Finally getting to the top of the biggest building, the cutscene forces you to jump off and fly away before you have a chance to explore. Had to reclimb to look around before finally jumping out of free will.

Should buy?

Yes, if you can deal with the jank. It's a nice and long zombie game, imo worth playing and enjoying, but please don't pay full price for this.

The developers of the original Modern Warfare 2 (the 2009 one) said that they ran into a problem after that game, because it was fundamentally an incredible game... but nobody knew why. Thus, they couldn't replicate that magic, because they didn't know what caused it in the first place.

I feel that Dying Light 1 create this same problem. In many ways, DL2 is fundamentally superior, with smoother animations, more zombie variety, more fleshed out character upgrades, and a more developed, interesting world. It has it faults as compared to DL1 (no grappling hook and no guns come to mind), but in most respects, it should be the superior game to DL1... but it's not. There's simply a magic about DL1 which they couldn't replicate this time around. DL2 is fleshed out and well made. It's not buggy or un-optimized, and Techland certainly did enough with it to claim it to be its own AAA game. But it's no DL1.

Is DL2 worth buying? Sure. I got my money's worth out of it and don't regret buying it. But don't go in expecting to re-live the magic of DL1. Think of it as its own standalone game, and you'll probably have a better time.

First off, I want to state: This game is MOSTLY amazing. No, I am not doing some meme or am an idiot for pressing "Not recommended", I am being honest. I loved a lot about this game. The atmosphere, the story, the side quests, the parkour, the music, hell even the characters. So why am I not recommending it?

It's because this isn't Dying Light. I basically wanted Dying Light 1 with a block button so 
human enemies don't make me wanna wring my own neck. I somewhat got that, but they changed too much. They went from what was meant to be, essentially, a horror game/semi RPG parkour game into a full-blown RPG parkour game.
I liked it in Dying Light 1 when at the end of the game, the zombies were a non-threat on the hardest difficulty. It made it feel like you became overpowered beyond belief, capable of literally instant killing a group of enemies with your bare fists, only the special infected being able to stand a chance. And even then, you can overcome them easily too. It made me feel like I earned that power, y'know? Cause it didn't happen instantly.

In this? There is no instant killing zombies anymore. It's all RPG. Each individual zombie has a healthbar and they *cannot* die until it empties. There's no getting a machete and feeling the satisfaction of just cutting off 5 heads at once, no throwing a grenade and seeing the bodies scatter in all their gory beauty. No, hit this zombie with your axe repeatedly until it falls over, like you're cutting away at a tree. And god forbid you play on Hard difficulty where the zombies are bullet sponges in the beginning of the game. Speaking of which...

Difficulty doesn't matter. I liked how in Dying Light you got rewards for beating the game on certain difficulties and how the most powerful items (Gold tier) ONLY dropped on the hardest one. It gave you a reason to play it. So in NG+ in DL2, I excitedly turned on Hard difficulty hoping to get some good shit. The bullet sponge enemies made me look up if Hard mode was even worth it. And uh... there are no rewards.

Let me repeat that: [b]THERE ARE NO FUCKING REWARDS![/b] Sure, harder difficulties don't need to make the game have more, better items. But Dying Light 1 had it, why not 2? For what purpose?? You don't even get more XP either. All it does is make the game a tedious slog. And from what I've read online? After getting around 6 skill points, you can instantly kill the zombies anyways so what's the point?

Onto my other criticism: THE FUCKING PARKOUR. Now for the eagle-eyed (Or rather, people with a 30 second attention span) you might notice I praised it earlier. Yeah, I did. It's fun. It has a lot of moves. And that's the problem. It's way too complicated. Sure, if you learn how it works then yeah it's functional but before then? Enjoy accidentally triggering wall-runs and tic tacs and falling off buildings. And the overly-complicated parkour also means doing simple things, like climbing through a fucking hole, can lead to your death (I speak from experience, it took me 20 minutes. Every time I tried to vault through, I would go too far and fall off the fucking scaffolding). It also meant I beat the entire game not knowing I could do an air kick or a rotate jump (Even though I had them unlocked), sure the air kick was on me but I never felt the need to do an air kick or a rotate jump anyways. Air Kick didn't feel like it was dealing enough damage (In the late game anyways, I only realized I could do it *after* the final boss so that's when I tested it) and rotate jump felt like the most situational skill in any game ever. Speaking of not dealing enough damage: Parkour Combat in general! They added it in. It was a fun gimmick, but just like the above? Next to useless. Hitting with a katana I found dealt more damage in one hit than my Vault Kick did in three, so why should I do that?

On the topic of weapons, here's another criticism: I nearly never needed to switch weapons out after I started getting Artifact-tier weapons. Cause I was getting them quicker than I was using them up. Yeah, and artifact tier is the highest rarity (not counting Legendary, as those are in NG+ which I only started recently). I wondered why they made it so weapons don't drop from human enemies anymore, but it's cause there's an over-abundance of them already. You become too powerful too quickly for it to be fun, except with throwing weapons which are next-to-useless. Which goes for the inhibitors too. Just put them all into stamina until you get about 220, then you've become unstoppable basically. And it also becomes a non-issue (Unless a specific safehouse or facility needs over that amount) as well, you can climb up an entire skyscraper with stamina to spare if you just wait a few seconds between the climbs.

Oh there's also the massive issue of nighttime as well. Stop me if you've heard this before: They are no longer risk vs reward systems in the early game unlike in Dying Light 1, they are practically recommended. The streets are dangerous, full of zombies and Howlers can get Virals or Volatiles to chase you. But if you stay on the rooftops (Which is piss-easy) you can avoid 95% of the Howlers. So you get double XP in parkour, at the cost of basically being unable to go down on the street (Which... why would you do that anyways during the night?) so they really just... removed most of the point honestly. Also, most special infected *only* come out at nighttime. I played through the entire game and only saw A SINGLE FUCKING BANSHEE. A SINGLE ONE. AND IT WAS THE TUTORIAL FOR THE SPECIALS. And do mind, I ran around A LOT during nighttime cause I realized it was basically free XP. So all of the new types? Yeah I didn't see most of them besides their few appearances in the main story (I mean, a Demolisher only shows up once as a boss battle and never again). And yes, I went to a lot of encounters and not a single one had a Demolisher. In fact, the special infected encounters never showed up a single time in my playthrough. Maybe it was bugged?

Speaking of bugs (I am really overusing this segue, I apologize), this game must've fucking been co-developed by Bethesda. I've had bugs of location markers teleporting 2 kilometers away after setting them down on a windmill only 100 meters from me, zombies running up to me and looking around before going un-alert (With me still infront of them) so I can just do a takedown, I fell through the floor once and died during the X13 quest, merchants sometimes just t-posed in the merchant screen, my character lost all animation in the equipment and skills screen and stood stiller than a Weeping Angel, I literally managed to rocket jump up to the rocket silo at the end of the game (During one of the endings) using my fucking grappling hook (I scaled the entire rocket chamber with a single grappling hook press??), a volatile spawned in a safehouse and died instantly, I could fucking go on honestly. This isn't an early access amount of bugs, but there were way too many. I remember I once hit a Peacekeeper with a fucking katana sword, cutting him in half, only for his friends to rush over, look at his body and fucking say "Must've been the wind" before returning to their business, even though I was standing right next to them.

This game is a bit of a disappointment but no by much. I probably will play more in my spare time (Most likely stream it to my boyfriend via Discord), but when I boot the game up there is absolutely 0 guarantee I will enjoy it.

Dying Light 2 had a lot of potential, especially given the success of its predecessor, but unfortunately, it falls short in several key areas. One of the most glaring issues is the sheer number of bugs and glitches. From broken quests to characters getting stuck or vanishing altogether, these technical problems severely disrupted the gameplay and immersion.

Beyond the bugs, the game quickly starts to feel repetitive. Despite a promising open-world setting, most missions boil down to similar objectives, and the once-thrilling parkour loses its charm after hours of doing the same movements. The combat, while satisfying at times, also becomes stale without much variety or progression.

Perhaps the most disappointing aspect, though, is the story. What starts with intrigue soon becomes predictable, with twists that you can see coming a mile away. Character choices that are supposed to matter often feel hollow, and the narrative lacks the emotional punch needed to keep you invested.

Overall, Dying Light 2 feels like a missed opportunity. It had the foundation for something great, but a lack of polish and depth turns it into a frustrating and forgettable experience.

Dying Light 2 isn't a terrible game, but it's one that's hard to recommend three years out from release, because a lot of the "day one roughness" never got fixed- or, indeed, feels like it's maybe even gotten worse.
Playing through a quest? Sometimes, NPCs or even doors will say "Please wait." However, as far as I can tell, waiting has never fixed this, at least not in the "stand there and wait for it to resolve" sense. What can fix it is leaving the area and coming back, because it looks like what's happening is the game doesn't load a state properly and instead of ever resolving just gives up. 
Physics is fun, and one of the highlights of the game when you drop kick an enemy into a wall. Little less fun when you stagger an enemy *through* a wall, and their loot is lost forever. Fortunately it seems like the game will either retrieve them or force kill them so you don't end up stuck, unlike with quest givers, but there are a number of stuck spots- I've usually been able to get unstuck, but it's really immersion breaking in a parkour focused game to end up stuck between two objects floating two feet off the ground and have to mash keys until some combination of jumping and dodging and clambering works to get free.
Co-op is not the ideal way to experience this game either, unfortunately. Quests seem to break more often, but also a lot of actions pull players to each other, which can be disruptive if you're split off doing a fight and your co-op partner pulls you to a quest. Not the end of the world but it doesn't feel seamless, especially since a lot of things like even minor NPC dialogue pull you to your co-op partner.
Real world clock quests to grind faction reputation is also a thing, which is basically a way of saying "You're going to have to play for several weeks to actually access this content locked behind high ranks." Not sure that's a terrible sin, nothing in the NPC shops are so incredibly special that you would be missing out too much, but it does just feel like a padding technique.
Additionally, I seem to have more performance issues now than I did the first time I played the game, with random stuttering, weird performance, needing to kill and restart desktop window manager to use my taskbar after quitting the game, etc. I'm not sure what the culprit is, could be my system, might be a bit of rose tinted glasses in favor of the performance closer to release. 
Story is fine, it's a zombie sandbox story, don't expect too much and you'll be fine. Movement is pretty good, it definitely is a priority, and you can use tools like the glider and grappling hook to cheese annoying bits of some platforming segments so it's neat. But passable combat and a good-enough story don't make up for the fact that the game just feels rough to play mechanically. It feels like most of the updates since launch were simply pushing DLC (and admittedly some free content) but not addressing engine issues or bugs or whatever is causing the issues I'm still having. And it's a shame- there are some moments where the game does feel great, but unfortunately the grinding attrition of bugs and other issues just tallies up throughout until by the end it's more frustrating than not.

Dying Light 2 – A “Labor of Love” That Doesn’t Respect the Player

I wanted to like this game. I invested the time. I played it properly. I set a personal goal to complete the achievements and experience everything the game had to offer. What I got instead was a long list of bugs, design decisions, and broken systems that actively punish players who try to engage deeply with the game.

Let’s start with the biggest issue: achievements and progression. I have collected every single base-game memento required for the Archivist achievement. I verified this against multiple guides, lists, and community resources. I didn’t rush. I didn’t skip content. The achievement simply does not unlock. This is not player error — it’s a bug. Spending dozens of hours hunting collectibles only for the game to not register your accomplishment is beyond frustrating. It makes the entire effort feel pointless.

On top of that, the game is riddled with movement and traversal bugs — in a game where movement is supposed to be the core strength. I’ve been stuck in the floor after landing from jumps or boosting with the paraglider. During scripted running segments, the game randomly pulls your character backward, forcing you into a walking speed. Then, the moment the segment ends, you’re suddenly back to full free-roam speed. It’s jarring, immersion-breaking, and still not fixed.

The economy is completely broken. Selling weapons, gear, and valuables nets you literal pennies — items are reduced to one cent — while basic gear, weapons, and upgrades in shops cost thousands. To make matters worse, the stats on store-bought items are often objectively terrible, making the grind feel insulting rather than rewarding. There is zero balance between effort and payoff.

Enemy behavior is another major issue. Zombies don’t just chase you — they sprint, climb, flip, vault, and practically scale skyscrapers just to stay on you. This goes far beyond challenge and crosses into absurdity. When infected are more agile than the player in a parkour-focused game, something is fundamentally wrong with the design.

What makes all of this worse is the messaging. The studio pushed hard for players to vote the game as a “Labor of Love.” That claim rings hollow when long-standing bugs remain unfixed, achievements don’t unlock correctly, traversal glitches persist, and systems actively discourage completionists. It does not feel like the developers respect the time or effort of players who commit to fully finishing the game.

I’ve been patient. I gave this game multiple chances. I pushed through issues because I genuinely wanted to complete it fairly. I did what the game asked of me — and it still failed to acknowledge that work. At a certain point, it feels like the game doesn’t want you to leave, because the moment you’re about to uninstall, it withholds the final confirmation that your effort mattered.

I cannot recommend this game. Not to completionists. Not to achievement hunters. Not even to players who just want a smooth parkour experience. Dying Light 2 consistently underachieves where it matters most, and no amount of updates or marketing can excuse systems that fundamentally do not work as intended.

This isn’t a labor of love. It’s a lesson in how quickly goodwill can be burned.

I'm glad I waited three and a half years after the game's release to play it, because by now most of the infuriating critical bugs have been fixed, numerous optimizations have been implemented overall, and some interesting new content has been added. All in all, it offers a much better experience compared to launch. That said, some noticeable bugs still linger. While they don't severely impact gameplay, they do slightly detract from the overall experience—like rain falling indoors in enclosed spaces, or previously explored locations still displaying question marks on the map, among other quirks.

From a gameplay perspective, it's fair to say DL2 builds upon its predecessor with richer content. Both combat and parkour have gained numerous engaging additions, while many minor details have been further refined, delivering a more exhilarating play experience. Ultimately, this is largely due to standing on the shoulders of giants. The foundational excellence of DL1 provided ample room for DL2 to build upon. However, some additions feel redundant or overly complex—at least not universally appreciated. Take the bounty mission system: designed to sustain long-term engagement, it even introduces daily and weekly objectives. Yet clearly, not everyone appreciates this overly structured, work-like routine. So while it appears to be a major feature of DL2, a portion of players simply won't enjoy this aspect. Thankfully, we're finally spared from things like DL1's “Hellraid.” Honestly, DL1 is a perfect game in my book overall—except for the “Hellraid” segment, which I'd give a 3/10 at best.

From a narrative standpoint, while it can't compare to DL1, DL2's story itself isn't bad. Overall, it tells a complete, self-contained tale with a logical beginning and end, and some NPC characterizations are quite memorable. However, this apocalyptic theme is incredibly clichéd. Countless outstanding works have explored similar subjects decades before DL2's 2022 release. Thus, players eagerly anticipate how such a well-worn topic can be presented with freshness and compelling storytelling. Unfortunately, I must say DL2's narrative leans toward the mundane—not terrible, but lacking any real brilliance. Interestingly, I guessed many of the plot twists and mysteries early on. By the time they were revealed in the mid-to-late game, my reaction was simply, “Oh, so that's how it is. Not surprising at all.” Even more curiously, some of its narrative techniques and character dialogue felt eerily reminiscent of common anime tropes. Many scenes made me feel like I was playing a JRPG or watching Japanese anime... I wonder if I'm the only one who felt this way.

All in all, despite its flaws, DL2 remains an unmissable masterpiece. After three and a half years of patches and refinements, the current version offers a relatively polished experience. But perhaps it's because DL1 delivered such immense shock and delight back then, becoming a monumental masterpiece in the hearts of many players, including myself. That's why we tend to scrutinize DL2 with stricter and more critical eyes. Regardless, I still highly recommend DL2 to every player who loved DL1.
