I actually played DL2 when it was released and played a solid 11 hours on it but for some reason it didn’t hold me. My memory doesn’t go that far back but I do remember the nights being fairly lackluster rather than the terrifying extended stealth endeavor that they were in the first game. The howlers replaced the deadly volatiles and started chases that were ultimately made the night more annoying to traverse than exciting. Ultimately my interests ended up drifting elsewhere, leading to a pretty quick uninstall. Last month they added the 1.11 “Good Night, Good Luck” update which removed howlers (they still prowl around here and there to spit at you) and gave the night back to volatiles. You’d think a nearly unkillable beast prowling the night would make the game less enjoyable but... that’s not the case.

I will say they did make the early game a bit overwhelming. As you don’t fully have the tools available to help you run away from them. Many of the early-game missions force the night upon you, unlike the gradual reveal the first game gave us. So newer players might have a rough time but luckily, I’m not fresh off the boat here. I played and beat the first game and I had some previous experience with Old Villedor, and while I was indeed overwhelmed at times with volatiles being in my way during important story missions, I wasn’t ever killed by one outright. So this update brought DL2 back to the first game’s roots, which was excellent.

So game-wise, for any potential newcomers from the update (and I know I’m a month late here), what we have here is a parkour hack and slash adventure with RPG elements and zombies. The RPG elements are second-note here, your leveling up just mostly gives you a multitude of traversal and combat abilities to make playing a bit easier over time. Later on you are given “Legend” levels, which act like paragon points from other games that just add raw percentages to your weapon damage which in turn allows you to take on those pesky volatiles with increasing regularity.

Ultimately the game is a lot of jumping and climbing but there’s two settings that can help newer players, letting the controls respond more automatically rather than constant inputs. For me it’s muscle memory at this point so I leave it on the more responsive mode that requires more inputs. I always just end up holding C when I fall off a ledge as it activates the landing roll which negates damage.

The gameplay loop is somewhat familiar to any Ubi-like players. There’s towers yes but later in the game and they’re mostly optional. At the time radio towers were unlocked, which were designed to help you locate the items that increase your health and stamina... I was already maxed out. There’s also windmills but they’re more important than they seem, because they not only give you one little safe zone. Unlocking them can also add 1-3 other safe zones in the immediate area (themed after which faction you end up siding with), which will always come in handy when running away from stuff in the night.

Another part of the loop is just looting buildings by day and hollows by night, as zombies have a behavior where they avoid the sun largely. So daytime is a bit emptier feeling than in the first game while at night it’s much livelier, but also makes exploring buildings a bit easier. Unfortunately the tradeoff is that daytime is more boring than the first game.

My complaint with this style is that the gameplay loop becomes fairly same-y after a while. I’ve been recording my playthrough for youtube and man, there’s a lot of looking at boxes and pressing F to loot bracelets and wires. I’ve come to not even bother recording taking over most electrical stations or water towers because they’re just parkour puzzles without a lot of action happening. And they have variable complexity so it’s not fun to watch or to play when I’m standing around for three minutes scratching my head wondering where to go next. There’s a lot of that as well, the metros follow mostly the same layout so there’s nothing new to explore. It’s just hitting generators and looting backpacks.

The story shines a bit more here, and I feel there’s more of it. There is however a flaw in the writing that others may have already pointed out. There’s two major factions, the survivors and the Peacekeepers. The PK’s are coded as fascist-like but only through dialog. The first time you run into them they’re not committing any major crimes, the first cutscene they’re introduced they’re just roughing up some zombies. All their actual crimes happen off-screen when they attack the survivors to the point where I wonder if it’s really them at all. Early in the story the survivors lie to Aiden enough to the point of almost killing him multiple times (they’re introduced by lynching him), which eventually lose my sympathy very quickly when it comes time to choose which faction to hand major resources over to. My first playthrough is full Peacekeeper, all the way. I’ll explore the survivor side on the NG+ but I’ll miss killing Barney.

This is a lot of words to say: I really like the game now. I’m sticking with it and I actually want to see it through. I don’t know what all they changed beyond the night update when I was away from it for more than a year but I’m all about it, now. So, kudos to the team.

Dying Light 2 on its own is an ok-ish game, however it pales in comparison to its predecessor.

PROS:

1. Combat is more complex with parrying/dodging mechanics (especially when you combine them with various skills), leaving you with a variety of ways to approach fights.

2.  Plenty of side quests and objectives that suit various gameplays, whether you like combat or parkour more, you'll find a variety of things to do.

3. The game incorporates various mechanics such as puzzles and challenges which appeal to different audiences and offer a well rounded, more satisfying experience.

4. Later on into the game, you'll have access to weapons that are strong enough to make quick work of the level 1 chumps wandering the streets, so you won't have to bother with them every time you go out. This was one of my main complains about DL1, where in the end game with fully upgraded high tier weapons, it took me 4-5 hits to take down an average walker.

5. The game has plenty of missions and objectives that can (only) be completed at night, which imo is a great ideea, as it forces you to step out of your confort zone and test your abilities, turning the night from dead-time to a productive and challenging time phase. You can even do those tasks during day time, which will turn the experience from challenging to brutal, for those who are looking for an adrenaline rush.

6. Both infected and human enemies are a lot more diverse, encouraging (but not forcing) you to keep a versatile arsenal of weapons on your character, suitable for any situation you might get yourself into.


CONS:

1. The overall athmosphere feels dull and boring, throwing away the entire ideea of a zombie apocalypse. I don't know why they chose to make everything so colorful, to me it just ruins the entire vibe and makes me feel like I'm in a cartoon. 

2. The characters are shallow and uninteresting, to the point where I just skipped dialogues simply because they were so lifeless and unnecessary.

3. The game offers you choices in both dialogues and actions, however Tachland really went overboard with the whole ideea of choice, so much so that every dialog line offers you multiple choices, which is annoying. Not every little thing has to be a choice...

4. Your choices don't really matter except for a few decisions.

5. The story is TERRIBLE and full of nonsense. 

6. The game is rather buggy, me myself encountering bugs that forced me to quit and start the game again because I got stuck in a random spot in between two objects, without any way of breaking free. I've also encountered some other minor bugs that I'll not mention but yeah, bugs are definitely present.

7. Gameplay is repetitive, once you have completed an objective of each type, you've basically completed them all...

8. The skill tree is full of skills that you will probably never use. Some of them are helpful and/or fun, however most of them feel unnecesary or very situational and you will probably forget about them all togheter...

9. TOO MANY GOD DAMN CUTSCENES.

This is more Dead Island than Dying Light. It seems to be a downgrade from the first game in most aspects. There are clear signs of either poorly rebuilt mechanics or simply poor design decisions. It could be the new engine, or it could just be due to all of the behind-the-scenes issues it had.

[b]The parkour[/b] lacks a flow that the first game had, providing instead janky animations and frustrating climbing systems. It feels floatier, which is fine, but it also feels more weightless, in the sense that you have less impact in the world when it comes to movement. This stems from constant hover hands, grabbing onto invisible objects, and odd animation blending when it comes to running/falling.

[b]The physics[/b] in general have been scaled back, there is far much less ragdolling with the environment. If you kick a zombie climbing up a building, instead of falling naturally, they play a stumble animation in mid-air and then plummet. You had this right in 2014, what happened there? While the combat against human AI has improved, the combat against the zombies has become much more numbing because of this. No longer will they ragdoll off of buildings, or through windows. These are now replaced with strict animations that only trigger the 'ragdoll' if a certain threshold is met, like it takes the AI a second to say "oh crap, there's no ground underneath me!" It gives the world a lot less of a presence, no longer having enemies trip over objects or fall with force.

[b]The story[/b] is extremely dull with continued exposition and lampshading that just reek of poor writing experience. The voice acting for the majority of the NPCs is extremely comical, with lousy exaggerations of American accents done by people who clearly aren't that. Harran had a pretty consistent cast of voice actors, if not in quality, in terms of the accents themselves given its middle-east/slavic setting. I don't know if there is an in-universe explanation as to this yet, but regardless, I just find hearing guys who sound like Solid Snake and Pvt. Pyle giving anime dubs extremely off-putting. This compounded with the dreadful dialogue makes the NPCs a headache, and the main villain is a bright example of this. Our introduction is him going into a monologue about his father and a farm as he's about to execute a nameless NPC we knew for 3 minutes. This is meant to be played as a completely serious dramatic moment, funny enough. It doesn't have the charm that the first game did, it's just downright incoherently insufferable at times. The first game's writing was laughably entertaining in its mediocrity, but this just makes you frustratingly bored.

[b]The combat[/b] lacks weight that the first game had, hits just seem to slide right through enemies without any real feedback. Once you kill them, they play one of a few death animations, or go flying weightlessly back. Dying Light had some exaggerated kills, but those zombies had weight to them. They'd knock other zombies down. It felt less like they were weightless, and more like you were just so strong that they'd get launched. The biggest example of this lack of feedback is the blood and gore, which has been hugely downgraded. Kill a zombie in the first game, and you can continue to beat its corpse as blood continues to splatter around. In this game, there are no real blood effects aside from pooling and the occasional splatter textured to the ground that only comes from when the enemy is still alive. It's odd, because the particle effects are a lot better and there's a lot of blood and viscera flying around, it just never seems to land anywhere.


I really wanted to like this game, it's why I gave it the full two hours before considering a refund. Maybe there's just something that clicks later on, but I just didn't get it. The game felt underwhelming, enough so that I decided to not carry forward with it. That could change after a few key patches, but for now, the game's backbone just isn't strong enough. That's what this entire review should be taken as, really. Not someone who has played or experienced the entire game's content and is giving a full critique, but of someone who played and experienced the very core mechanics, and was none too impressed to carry on with them for the rest of the game. I haven't unlocked all of the skills, or traveled along the cityscape, or made any impactful story decisions. That's why I haven't commented on it, for all I know it can be great.

What I have seen, though, I don't know. This is nowhere on the levels of Cyberpunk in terms of disappointment, but it does seem to be that these once renowned Polish studios are simply losing their touch. It's not insultingly underwhelming, just viciously mediocre, especially when you compare its predecessor which was quite innovative for its time. This game seems to rehash current industry tropes rather than capitalizing on creating future ones. I could see it improving down the line. If anything, Techland are known for supporting their existing games, with Dying Light still receiving updates to this day. The story however, seems to just be a cliche mess of poorly thought out ideas that never once manages to hit proper beats enough to grasp for your attention. It could be it rises out of the ashes some time later on, but that kind of defeats the purpose of creating a strong opening. You want a hook, you want strong characters, and you want something to keep the player going, even a single reason to give a damn and push forward. That was not achieved for me, and the gameplay simply wasn't strong enough yet to risk the gamble of the game being nothing more than 50 hours of the same exact issues.

Wait for a sale on this one and try it for yourself, otherwise you too may be stopping yourself after your second hour to spend your money on something more worth it.

I think TechLand actually shot themselves in the foot with Dying Light 2 by making Dying Light first.

As a standalone game, Dying Light 2 is great. The combat (at least on your end) is interactive with multiple moves and skills, the parkour itself is hella enjoyable and responsive, if a bit floaty at times, and the story is reasonable, given the fact that multiple of the lead story writers left during development.

The problems start when you compare it to the original Dying Light. They hit the nail on the head with the gameplay and combat in the original, to a point where the sequel feels like a downgrade in some areas. The story is considerably worse in comparison, and although the first games story wasn't the best, the characters actually showed emotion through their movements and voices. In the first game, Kyle Crane who was a government operate found himself whisked away in the drama of Harran, his goals and personality changing as he stopped listening to those who controlled him, breaking free and developing independence. Meanwhile Aiden Caldwell doesn't give much of a shit about what's going on in Old Villedor, only using it and its people as a means find his sister.

One other point of comparison that I won't delve too much into right now is the 'Ubisoftification' of the franchise in the sequel. Things like thousands of collectables and unreasonable costs for upgrading things.

By itself, a great game, but left in the shadow of its predecessor.

TL;DR: This is not Dying Light 2, its a Ubisoft-Zombie-Parkour RPG. 

Im left with this sour taste in my mouth that the directors just looked at other popular RPGs and copied their systems, not even once stopping to consider why or what, and if a certain mechanic even made sense in the world of Dying Light. As if mechanics just got introduced for no reason other than "all the other games are doing it nowadays".

The mechanics fall into the god-awful, painstakingly mediocre trope of modern RPGs, softlocked regions and areas, the former through enemies now having stat levels, and the latter being inaccessible with the introduction of a depleting stamina meter while climbing. There's way more examples, and I think the key point is that the design of these mechanics all make up a fairly decent game, but they are SO far fetched from what ultimately makes up the core identity of Dying Light, that this experience just doesnt feel like I'm playing Dying Light, but some Zombie-RPG. 

Needless integration of modern RPG elements that didn't see a shred of light in the first instalment litter this game. Abundance of minimap clutter, every minuscule event/location has its own unique icon which leads to an overwhelming experience while somehow making it feel like the game is holding my hand simultaneously. The inventory UI has devolved from "unique and easy to read" into "every RPG developed in the past three years" and the skill trees are somehow smaller and less inspired. 

Zones/regions are softlocked by the joyous system of enemy levels, and every fathomable enemy now has a level, health bar and stamina bar (granted the UI can be turned off but the system of softlocking progress through levelling falls right into the common trope of the every modern RPG game) 

Movement is clunky and somehow feels slow. I get stuck on ledges and the animations feel stiff, jittery and uncomfortable at the same time, not to mention that climbing is now tied to a depleting stamina bar. Meaning that if I want to climb somewhere cool, I first have to go scour for syringes to up my stamina meter.

I'm still fairly early in my playthrough but I still believe that this critique is fair, as the thoughts proposed all revolve the games' core and as such, definitely wont be subject to change in the future.

All right game, but not a Dying Light game.

This is the biggest disappointment in recent memory. I can't help but feel like all the positive reviews were written by whoever decided to write up the NPCs. I absolutely loved Dying Light 1. Plot: I couldn't stomach more than 3 hours so I don't know if it gets any better, but the beginning is riddled with laughably bad dialog, tired "outsider bad" victim mentality motifs you'd see in a teen drama novel, a main character so unlikable that I felt tempted to leap from buildings just to spite him, and plot hooks that were just genuinely uninteresting. [h1][b]1.Introduction[/b][/h1]
[b]Dying Light 2 (DL2) is an amazing experience which massively improves upon the formula of the first game (Dying Light – DL1).[/b] [b]Unfortunately, the reception of the game was in part mixed [/b]because of nostalgia-blinded fans of the first game who can't accept even the slightest changes from the original formula.

[b][i][u]Some on the other hand are mad the game doesn't look and play exactly like an early tech demo that was shown in 2019. [/u][/i][/b]I describe the E3 trailer “drama” in detail later.

[h1][b]2.Story (no spoilers)[/b][/h1]
[b]The plot in this game is nothing special (it's hard to innovate in the zombie genre) but it's engaging thanks to impactful choices, well-written characters, the overall atmosphere, and fantastic gameplay.[/b] The beginning and the middle of the story are the most interesting – I really like how the game introduces all factions and overall state of the society of Villedor while combining it with the personal agenda of Aiden (the main protagonist).

[b]The ending part feels unfortunately rushed. [/b]So far, I have seen 4 endings – all of them were quite different. [b]Achieving some of them is not just a matter of making a single choice at the end of the game.[/b]

[h1][b]3.Characters[/b][/h1]
[b]I really enjoy the characters in this game.[/b] A lot of them are definitely not one-dimensional and not necessarily good or evil. Many of them have also not-so-obvious backstory that explains their behavior and choices in a satisfying way. In the case of some (especially Hakon and Lawan), it really takes some time to get to know them better.

[b]The voice acting is very, very good[/b] – you can really feel Lawan's concern mixed with anger towards Aiden, you can really feel the easy-going nature of Hakon during friendly banter between him and Aiden, you can really feel how much Sophie wants to help the Survivors.

[b]Jonah Scott (voice actor for the main protagonist) did an exceptional job.[/b] He can be tough and vulnerable, very serious and hilarious, witty and cocky but also mature. His grunts and efforts during combat and parkour are well done.

[h1][b]4.Graphics and overall atmosphere[/b][/h1]
Overall, the [b]game looks fantastic and presents a unique “middle post-apo” style.[/b] What do I mean by that? For me, Fallout 3 and Mad Max represent “high post-apo” (utter destruction of the former world), while DL1 represents “young post-apo” (isolated city 3 months after zombie pandemic). In DL2 society came back to life and is used to living in the ruins of the former world.

[b]I especially love how nature “took over” the city.[/b] You see small trees growing on top of high buildings, vines covering walls, grass growing on roads among the cars etc. It looks beautiful, but at the same time reminds you that the former world is gone.

[h1][b]5.Soundtrack[/b][/h1]
[b]As was the case with the first game, Techland again nailed it with the soundtrack. [/b]DL2 catches vibe of the first game but also evolves on it, giving a more “mature” vibe. It's also more varied – simply check out some examples ([url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5vRnzgcy7hA&list=PLTmJuovQUxPsWEFVC5lEKvBHl4za1Och0&index=17]combat[/url], [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ssbu-MZo0VA&list=PLTmJuovQUxPsWEFVC5lEKvBHl4za1Och0&index=12]parkour[/url], [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XvzldR-E6jI&list=PLTmJuovQUxPsWEFVC5lEKvBHl4za1Och0&index=21]serious/dramatic moments[/url]).

[b]Music is very well used during story moments to amplify certain emotions. [/b]I would also like to really praise [b]parkour tracks dedicated to making the process of traversing the city even more empowering.[/b]

[h1][b]6.Creative, brutal and impactful first-person combat[/b][/h1]
[b]The combat in Dying Light 2 is spectacular.[/b] There are not many games that focus on [b]first-person melee combat combined with very fluid and advanced movement.[/b]

Once you get a hold of the system and start combining different moves, tools, consumables, weapon mods and elements of the environment [b][i]you can really feel like a ninja that strikes fast and is uncatchable. [/i]Unfortunately, the[/b] [b]ragdoll system isn't as good as in the first game.[/b]

[h1][b]7.How parkour and level design make literally everything better[/b][/h1]
[b]Dying Light 2 is[/b] [b]one of the most unique AAA games in many years in terms of gameplay because it turned the simple activity of moving around the world to a fantastic journey of skill and flow. [/b]As someone who has spent hundreds of hours in every possible game with advanced movement systems, [b][i][u]I am ready to die defending this opinion – this game offers the best parkour system in the history of gaming and for many years nothing will top it.[/u][/i][/b]

Developers literally doubled or even tripled possible parkour moves compared to the first game. The way you can combine all of them is amazing.

[b][i][u]What counts the most, however, is the overall genius of "level design parkour optimization".[/u][/i][/b] [b][i][u]I swear – sometimes I can't tell whether I am so good at parkour or is the city literally putting on all the ledges, ropes, platforms, lamps, and windows as I go so, I can keep the flow.[/u][/i][/b]

Literally [b]even the simplest fetch quest can be very interesting because of all the moment-to-moment journey you experience thanks to the movement system.[/b]

[h1][b]8.That damn E3 trailer[/b][/h1]
In case you don't know, the thing that hyped and marketed Dying Light 2 the most was 25 minutes long 2019 E3 gameplay trailer. What's the problem with it? [b][i][u]Some people were dumb enough to expect the final game to look exactly like a 3-years-old scripted, color corrected, run in-engine, and even edited/cut at one point trailer.[/u][/i][/b]

[b]And no, Techland didn't try to cover things up and make false promises.[/b] The recent trailers released in mid/end of 2021 showed the game just as it is. Before the release, many content creators were even able to play extensive demos and show the gameplay.

Why am I mentioning this? Because Dying Light 2 overall is a fantastic game. Many, however, before the release were still expecting the E3 trailer fantasy. [b]Since it didn’t realize fully, they can’t shut up about it and treat DL2 as a failure, completely overlooking the things it got right – [/b]keep that in mind while reading other reviews.

[h1][b]9.Summary[/b][/h1]
Dying Light 2 is my favourite game of the year. If you are looking for something that offers unique gameplay, try it out. Definitely grab it on good sales.

You can read my more in-depth review of the game [url=https://docs.google.com/document/d/1i7fLNnkJDpbyMbH2B9tJAm-5vAwDvpQn/edit#heading=h.30j0zll][b]here[/b][/url] – I provide tips on how to enjoy the game more as well as a list of useful mods.

Story time: A very long time ago I tried the first Dying Light and really did not enjoy it for some reason. Time passed and I gave it a second shot, and I really ended up enjoying it! Of course I had to give Dying Light 2 a try after that. I did, and I got too distracted with side content and ended up being bored. Fast-forward to present time, where I decided to give Dying Light 2 another try. 

What did I think?

I really did not expect to like this game that much. I liked it so much that I added it to my favourites list on Steam, which might not mean much to you, but it definitely does to me. 

Not many open-world games have worlds that are actually fun to traverse, but man the parkour in Dying Light 2 is SO GOOD. Dying Light 2 has actually earned the right to call its open world a playground, because you can *actually* play in it. As you unlock more parkour abilities, you realize that previously innocent-looking objects simply populating the environment can be fully utilized to speed up traversal and make it flow. Waist-high walls can suddenly be used either for super jumps or fast dashes forward, you begin to look at walls differently once you unlock wall-running, and even doing air takedowns on enemies can be taken into consideration when you need to drop down from heights. The world is designed around the gameplay and vice versa, making the whole game feel like a smooth experience.

Of course it helps that the combat is very fun. Updates have added a bunch of things to spice it up. Once again, there's plenty of abilities to unlock, and again, some of these can be utilized in your traversal of the open world.

But one thing I definitely did not expect was how good the music was. This is not just a case of "wow this song's pretty good," the soundtrack is incredibly well-produced and really enhances the atmosphere of the game. 

Without spoiling too much, there is a sequence in the game where you have to climb the tallest structure in the city. The song that plays here is up there among my favourite songs in a video game of all time. At this point in the game, you should have most of the parkour abilities unlocked. As you climb closer towards the skies with the hopeful music slowly ramping up in intensity, it hits you: 

You've grown. You're stronger. 

Call me crazy, but I consider this moment one of the strongest arguments for why video games are art. Sure, the presentation and music is great, but this moment hits hard because you are straight up using abilities to perform a feat that you could not earlier. 

It's not just "oh I can use a super attack now to kill this boss." 

Every single input you do is meaningful in how your character moves, and at the end of it all, not only has your character finally reached the top of the world... 

So have you. 

Many agree that video games have the advantage of being interactive media. Many also agree that video games are art. Yet, I never hear anyone talking about how the interactivity contributes to games being art. While I haven't thought about that question much myself either, I definitely will after Dying Light 2.
